blocks.text: 1. Memory
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447722250-513780180.png

Reflection closed by extending its evaluative check to the complete final answer. Memory, retaining information across steps and conversations, closes the trio of planning, reflection, and memory that Tool Calling named as built on top of the basic tool calling mechanism.
It stores facts learned earlier so later steps and later conversations can actually reuse them.
2. Short-Term Memory Within One Conversation
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447722250-173918144.png
Within one ongoing conversation, each earlier tool result stays available to later steps, the same mechanism as feeding the result back to the model in Tool Calling.
This short-lived, within-session memory is the simplest form of retained state.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Memory type","How long it persists"],"rows":[["Short-term","Only within the current conversation"],["Long-term","Across separate, later conversations"]]}

blocks.text: 3. Long-Term Memory Across Conversations
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447722250-22086819.png
Information worth keeping beyond a single conversation needs to be written to persistent storage.
A later, entirely separate conversation can then read that same stored fact back.
4. What To Store Versus What To Discard

blocks.alt: What To Store Versus What To Discard
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447722251-916681381.png
Not every detail from a conversation is worth retaining long-term, the same discipline as context filtering in Context Management.
A deliberate filter decides what actually gets written to persistent memory.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A one-off typo the user corrected mid-conversation does not belong in long-term memory, while a stated preference like preferred communication style does, the same deliberate filtering as context filtering.

blocks.text: 5. Retrieving Relevant Memories, Not All Of Them

blocks.alt: Retrieving Relevant Memories, Not All Of Them
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447722251-360587680.png
Stored memories are retrieved by relevance to the current query, not loaded in full every time, the same idea as semantic search in Retrieval.
Memory retrieval is itself a retrieval problem, using the same techniques covered elsewhere in this course.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Approach","What gets loaded"],"rows":[["Load all stored memories","Every past fact, regardless of relevance"],["Retrieve relevant memories","Only memories relevant to the current query"]]}

blocks.text: 6. Memory Enables Personalization Over Time
A fact learned in one conversation, such as a stated preference, can shape how a later, separate conversation responds.
Without persistent memory, every conversation starts from a blank slate.
7. Stale Or Wrong Memories Cause Real Harm

blocks.alt: Stale Or Wrong Memories Cause Real Harm
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447722251-490847682.png
A stored fact that later becomes outdated misleads every future step that relies on it, the same propagation risk as an error in an early hop in Multi-Hop RAG.
Memory needs its own update and invalidation process, not just accumulation.

blocks.title: Note
blocks.content: A stored preference that a user later explicitly changes must overwrite the old stored value, or the assistant keeps acting on a fact that is no longer true, the same propagation risk described in Multi-Hop RAG.

blocks.text: 8. Memory Adds Storage And Retrieval Cost
Storing and later retrieving memories is its own infrastructure and latency cost, the same tradeoff as each added step costing latency in Advanced RAG.
It is a real investment beyond the within-session case alone.
9. Recognizing When Persistent Memory Earns Its Added Cost

blocks.alt: Recognizing When Persistent Memory Earns Its Added Cost
blocks.text: https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785447722251-628009737.png
An assistant serving the same user repeatedly benefits from persistent memory.
A one-off, single-session task, by contrast, needs only short-term, within-conversation memory.

blocks.text: 11. Common Mistakes

items: Storing every detail from a conversation instead of filtering for what is actually worth retaining.
Loading all stored memories into every prompt instead of retrieving only the relevant ones.
Never updating or invalidating a stored fact after the user changes it.
Adding persistent memory infrastructure to a one-off, single-session task that does not need it.

blocks.text: 12. Key Takeaways

items: Memory retains information across steps and across separate conversations.
Short-term memory lasts within one conversation; long-term memory persists across conversations.
A deliberate filter decides what is actually worth writing to persistent memory.
Stored memories are retrieved by relevance to the current query, not loaded in full every time.
A fact learned in one conversation, like a stated preference, can shape a later, separate conversation.
A stale stored fact misleads every future step that relies on it, just as an early hop error does.
Memory needs its own update and invalidation process, not just accumulation.
Storing and retrieving memories is its own real infrastructure and latency cost.
